a: Wisdom will sing her own praise
p: The Greek says Wisdom will "praise her soul", a Hebrew way of saying "praise herself".
b: The chapter opens with a heading, "The praise of Wisdom", and then lets Wisdom speak in her own voice, as in Proverbs 8, where Wisdom calls out at the city gates (Proverbs 8:1–3). The Greek ainesēsei psychēn autēs, "she will praise her soul", follows a Hebrew idiom in which "my soul" means "myself". The Plain writes "Wisdom" with a capital where she speaks or acts as a person, as the site does in Proverbs and the Wisdom of Solomon. No Hebrew copy of chapter 24 has been found, so the Greek of Ben Sira's grandson is the oldest text.
orig: Ἡ σοφία αἰνέσει ψυχὴν αὐτῆς (hē sophia ainesei psychēn autēs), 'Wisdom will praise her soul'
r: Proverbs 8:1–3; Proverbs 9:1–6; Proverbs 1:20–33; Wisdom of Solomon 7:22–8:1; Baruch 3:9–4:4

a: the assembly of the Most High
p: Wisdom speaks before God's heavenly court, or before Israel gathered for worship. The verse allows both.
b: "Her people" in 24:1 and "the assembly of the Most High" here could be Israel gathered to worship, the qahal of the Hebrew Bible, which the Greek calls ekklēsia. But the second line places her "before his armies", the Greek dynamis used for the host of heaven, and Psalm 82 pictures God standing "in the assembly of El" (Psalm 82:1). Many readers therefore take the scene as a heavenly court, with Wisdom speaking among the angels. The two need not exclude each other: Wisdom who lives in Israel (24:8–12) praises herself both on earth and in heaven.

a: I came out of the Most High's mouth
p: Wisdom comes from God's mouth, as his word does. Proverbs 2:6 says the same of knowledge and understanding.
b: Proverbs had said, "It is the LORD who gives wisdom; knowledge and understanding come out of his mouth" (Proverbs 2:6), and the psalm sings that "the heavens were made by the LORD's word" (Psalm 33:6). Ben Sira joins the two: Wisdom is like the breath or word that goes out of God's mouth. The mist that covers the earth may recall the waters of the first creation (Genesis 1:2) or the water that rose to water the ground (Genesis 2:6). Christian readers later heard in this verse the Word who "was with God" (John 1:1); the note on 24:8 weighs that link.
r: Proverbs 2:6; Psalm 33:6; Genesis 1:2; Genesis 2:6; Isaiah 55:11; John 1:1

a: I pitched my tent in the heights
p: The verb is "to pitch a tent". It runs through the chapter and is the word John 1:14 uses of the Word.
b: The Greek katēskēnōsa comes from skēnē, "tent", the Greek Old Testament's word for the tabernacle. The chapter keeps returning to it: Wisdom pitches her tent in the heights (24:4), God gives her tent a resting place and tells her to pitch it in Jacob (24:8), and she serves in "the holy tent" (24:10). The Plain keeps "tent" each time so the thread can be seen. The pillar of cloud is the cloud that went before Israel in the wilderness: "by day in a pillar of cloud to lead them along the road" (Exodus 13:21). Wisdom's throne is in the same cloud that marked God's presence with his people.

a: the circle of the sky
p: Wisdom walks the circle of the sky and the deep alone, places the Bible gives to God himself.
b: In Proverbs, Wisdom was present "when he carved a circle on the surface of the deep" (Proverbs 8:27). Job's friend pictures God who "strolls about on the rim of the sky" (Job 22:14), and God asks Job, "Have you walked about where the deep is deepest?" (Job 38:16). Ben Sira gives these journeys to Wisdom, "alone". He does not make her a second god, since she is "created" (24:9), but she goes where only God's own presence reaches.

a: In whose inheritance should I make my camp?
p: Wisdom searches the nations for a home and finds it in Israel. 1 Enoch tells the opposite story.
b: Wisdom has a share in every nation (24:6), yet she looks for one place to rest, and God sends her to Jacob (24:8). The book of 1 Enoch, part of the Bible of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, tells the reverse: "Wisdom found no place to live, so a home was made for her in the heavens"; she went out to live among people, "but she found no home" and went back to sit among the angels (1 Enoch 42:1–2). Baruch, like Ben Sira, says God gave her to "his servant Jacob" (Baruch 3:37). John's prologue uses a pattern close to Enoch's: the Word "came to what was his own", and his own did not receive him (John 1:11).

a: Pitch your tent in Jacob
t: "Pitch your tent in Jacob" and John 1:14
p: God tells Wisdom to pitch her tent in Israel. John says the Word "pitched his tent among us".
b: The command uses the same tent verb as 24:4, kataskēnōson. John's Gospel says of the Word: "the Word became flesh and pitched his tent among us. We gazed at his glory" (John 1:14). John's verb, eskēnōsen, is the same word without the prefix. Wisdom comes from God's mouth (24:3), exists from the beginning (24:9), lives with God's people and serves in his tent; John's Word was in the beginning with God and lived among people. Many scholars think John drew on this Jewish picture of Wisdom when he wrote his prologue. The difference is just as clear: Ben Sira says Wisdom became the book of the law (24:23); John says the Word "became flesh".
orig: Ἐν Ἰακὼβ κατασκήνωσον (en Iakōb kataskēnōson), 'in Jacob pitch your tent'

a: He created me before the ages
p: Like the Greek of Proverbs 8:22, Ben Sira calls Wisdom created. That mattered once Christians read Wisdom as Christ.
b: Agrees: Proverbs has Wisdom say, "The LORD acquired me, the first of his way, before his works of long ago" (Proverbs 8:22), and the Greek of Proverbs renders the verb "created". Ben Sira says the same plainly (24:9; compare 1:4). Wisdom is the first and oldest of God's works, not a second God. A question for Christian readers: once the church read the Wisdom of Proverbs 8 as the Son of God (1 Corinthians 1:24; Colossians 1:15), the word "created" became a point of dispute in the controversy over Arius in the 300s, and the Nicene Creed confesses the Son "begotten, not made". Ben Sira himself identifies Wisdom with the law (24:23), so most readers today take his "created" of God's wisdom given to Israel, not of a person beside the Father.

a: I served in worship before him in the holy tent
p: The Greek verb is the one used for the priests' service in the sanctuary.
b: Leitourgeō, "to serve in worship", is the Greek Old Testament's word for the work of priests and Levites at the tabernacle and temple; English "liturgy" comes from it. Wisdom is pictured doing priestly service, first in the tent in the wilderness and then in Zion. The spices of 24:15 are those of the holy incense, so the whole passage sets Wisdom inside Israel's worship. Ben Sira loved the temple and its priests: the book ends its Praise of the Fathers with the high priest Simon serving at the altar (chapter 50).

a: the city he loves
p: Jerusalem is the city God loves, as the psalms say of Zion.
b: The psalms speak of "Mount Zion, the one he loved" (Psalm 78:68) and say "the gates of Zion are what the LORD loves, more than all Jacob's dwellings" (Psalm 87:2). Ben Sira writes as a man of Jerusalem in the years after the temple had been repaired (50:1). For him, Wisdom does not float above the world: she has an address, the city and its temple.

a: in the Lord's portion, his inheritance
p: Israel is the Lord's own share among the nations, as the Song of Moses says.
b: The phrase takes up Deuteronomy 32:9: "For the LORD's own share is his people; Jacob is the inheritance measured out for him." The nations each had their share (Deuteronomy 32:8), but Israel was the Lord's. Wisdom roots herself in that people, and the word "inheritance" ties the passage together: she asks in whose inheritance to camp (24:7), receives Israel as her inheritance (24:8), is herself an inheritance (24:20), and becomes the law, "the heritage of the assemblies of Jacob" (24:23), the same Greek word.

a: Like a cedar in Lebanon I rose high
t: A map of the land in trees
p: The trees run from Lebanon and Hermon in the north to Jericho and the shore: Wisdom fills the land.
b: Ben Sira names the land's finest trees and places: the cedar of Lebanon and the cypress of Hermon in the far north, the palm of the coast (or of En-gedi, in some copies: see the variant at 24:14), the gardens of Jericho in the Jordan valley, the olive of the plain. The psalms use the same trees for the righteous: "The righteous will sprout like the date palm; like a cedar in Lebanon they will grow tall" (Psalm 92:12), and Hosea promises that Israel will put down roots "like Lebanon" (Hosea 14:5). Wisdom grows through the whole land like its best trees.
r: Psalm 92:12; Hosea 14:5–7; Numbers 24:6; Song of Songs 4:13–14

a: like galbanum, onycha and stacte
t: The spices of the holy incense
p: Wisdom smells like the incense of the tabernacle, made by the recipe in Exodus 30.
b: God told Moses, "Take spices: stacte, onycha and galbanum, spices mixed with pure frankincense, an equal part of each" (Exodus 30:34). Cinnamon also went into the holy anointing oil (Exodus 30:23). Aspalathus is a sweet-smelling thorny shrub. The last line places the smoke "in the tent", the tabernacle. Wisdom's fragrance is the fragrance of worship: where she lives, God is honored as in the sanctuary.
r: Exodus 30:23–25; Exodus 30:34–38; Song of Songs 4:14; Revelation 8:3–4

a: Like a vine I budded with grace
p: The vine was a picture of Israel. Jesus later says, "I am the real vine" (John 15:1).
b: The Hebrew Bible pictures Israel as a vine God brought out of Egypt: "A vine from Egypt you dug up and moved. You threw out nations, and you planted it" (Psalm 80:8), and Isaiah sings of God's vineyard (Isaiah 5:1–7). Here Wisdom, rooted in Israel, is the vine, and her fruit is glory and wealth. In John's Gospel Jesus says, "I am the real vine, and my Father is the farmer" (John 15:1). Christian readers who see Christ as God's Wisdom read the two together; the Jewish reading sees the Torah bearing fruit in Israel.

a: the mother of beautiful love
p: This line, missing from Vaticanus, is in the Latin. Catholic devotion took it as a title of Mary.
b: The verse belongs to the longer Greek text and the Latin (see the variant). In the Clementine Vulgate it is 24:24, Ego mater pulchrae dilectionis, et timoris, et agnitionis, et sanctae spei, which the Douay-Rheims renders "I am the mother of fair love, and of fear, and of knowledge, and of holy hope." Because the Church has long read the wisdom passages "in relation to Mary" (Catechism 721), the line became a Marian title, "Mother of Fair Love". St. Josemaría Escrivá had a strong devotion to Mary under this title, and Opus Dei keeps a feast of Mary, Mother of Fairest Love on February 14. In Ben Sira's own context the speaker is Wisdom, the mother of love, fear and hope in those who seek her.

a: Come to me, you who long for me
p: Wisdom invites the hungry, as in Proverbs 9. Jesus' "Come to me" in Matthew 11:28 has the same shape.
b: Wisdom in Proverbs sets her table and calls, "Come, have some of my bread, and drink the wine I mixed" (Proverbs 9:5); Isaiah calls, "All you who are thirsty, come to the water!" (Isaiah 55:1). Ben Sira's Wisdom calls in the same way. Jesus says, "Come to me, all of you who are worn out and loaded down, and I myself will give you rest" (Matthew 11:28), and he goes on to speak of his yoke, as Ben Sira does of Wisdom's yoke in chapter 51 (51:23–27). The book's opening pages weigh how strong the link is.

a: sweeter than honey
p: The psalm says the same of God's laws, which prepares for 24:23: Wisdom is the law.
b: Psalm 19 says of the LORD's rulings: "they are sweeter than honey, than what drips from the comb" (Psalm 19:10), and Psalm 119 adds, "How smooth your saying is to my palate, smoother than honey in my mouth!" (Psalm 119:103). Ezekiel ate God's scroll, "and in my mouth it was as sweet as honey" (Ezekiel 3:3). By using the honey image that belongs to God's law, Wisdom prepares for the turn of 24:23.

a: Whoever eats me will still be hungry
p: Wisdom's food makes people hungry for more. Jesus, the bread of life, says the one who comes to him "will not go hungry".
b: Agrees in spirit, differs in image: Ben Sira means that Wisdom is so good that those who taste her want more of her; the hunger is desire, not lack. Jesus turns the image the other way: "I am the bread of life. Anyone coming to me will not go hungry at all, and the one who believes in me will not thirst again, not ever" (John 6:35), and to the woman at the well, "whoever drinks from the water that I will give him will never, ever be thirsty" (John 4:14). Read side by side, the two sayings point opposite ways: what Wisdom makes people long for, Jesus says he satisfies. Whether John had this verse in mind cannot be shown; both draw on the old picture of wisdom as food and drink.

a: the book of the covenant of God Most High
p: Ben Sira names the Wisdom of the poem: she is the book of the law of Moses.
b: After Wisdom's speech, Ben Sira speaks in his own voice: "All these things" (everything Wisdom has said of herself) are "the book of the covenant", the law of Moses. The phrase recalls Exodus 24:7, where Moses "took the scroll of the covenant and read it out for the people". Deuteronomy already said that keeping the law "will show your wisdom and your understanding to the peoples" (Deuteronomy 4:6). Baruch says the same of Wisdom: "She is the book of the commands of God, the law that lasts forever" (Baruch 4:1). Readings: for Jewish readers this is the heart of the chapter, the Torah as God's own wisdom living in Israel. Christian readers who apply the poem to Christ or Mary (24:8; 24:18) read it as pointing beyond the law; critical scholars see Ben Sira joining Greek-age wisdom to the Jewish law.
r: Exodus 24:7; Deuteronomy 4:6; Deuteronomy 30:11–14; Baruch 4:1; Psalm 147:19–20; Galatians 3:24

a: the heritage of the assemblies of Jacob
p: The last line quotes the Greek of Deuteronomy 33:4 word for word. "Assemblies" is synagōgai, later "synagogue".
b: Moses' blessing begins, "Moses commanded us a law, the heritage of the assembly of Jacob" (Deuteronomy 33:4), and the Greek of Deuteronomy has the very words Ben Sira's grandson uses, klēronomian synagōgais Iakōb. The Plain follows Deuteronomy's English. The word rendered "heritage" is the same Greek word as "inheritance" in 24:7–20: Wisdom, who looked for an inheritance, is now Israel's inheritance. Synagōgē means a gathering; in the grandson's day Jews in Egypt and elsewhere met in houses of prayer, and the word came to name the building, the synagogue, as in the Gospels.

a: no other savior
p: This longer-text line echoes Isaiah's "There is no one but me who saves."
b: The line is not in Vaticanus (see the variant). It takes up the words of Isaiah: "I myself, I am the LORD. There is no one but me who saves" (Isaiah 43:11), and "There is no other god besides me, a God who is righteous and saves" (Isaiah 45:21). Coming right after the law of Moses, it reminds the reader that the law points to the one God who rescues.

a: like the Pishon
p: The law fills like the four rivers of paradise, with the Jordan added: Eden's water flows in Israel.
b: Genesis says that "a river goes out from Eden to water the garden" and divides into four: the Pishon, the Gihon, the Tigris and the Euphrates (Genesis 2:10–14). Ben Sira names all four and adds the Jordan, Israel's own river, which "runs full over all its banks the whole harvest season" (Joshua 3:15). Each river is tied to a season of flood: new fruit in spring, the grain harvest, the grape harvest in autumn. "It" is the law of 24:23: the masculine participles in the Greek point back to nomos, "law". Eden's abundance, lost in Genesis, flows again through the law in Israel.

a: It makes instruction shine out like light
p: The Greek says "like light". The Hebrew probably said "like the Nile", one letter different.
b: Every other line in 24:25–27 names a river, so "like light" stands out. Bullard and Hatton note that the Hebrew word for the Nile could easily be mistaken for the Hebrew word for "light", and that the Syriac version has the river. The Hebrew ye'or, "Nile" (also any stream), and 'or, "light", differ by one small letter, so the grandson, or the copy he used, probably read the second. The Plain keeps the Greek, since it is the text translated here. The Gihon in the next line is one of Eden's rivers, and the Greek of Jeremiah 2:18 already used the name Gihon for the Nile.
orig: ὡς φῶς (hōs phōs), 'like light'; Hebrew probably כַּיְאֹר (kay'or), 'like the Nile', read as כָּאוֹר (ka'or), 'like light'

a: The first person did not finish knowing her
p: "The first" may be Adam, or simply the first person who ever lived. No one, first or last, knows Wisdom fully.
b: The Greek ho prōtos, "the first", is often read as Adam, the first human, who did not come to know Wisdom fully; "the last" is the last person who will ever live. Others read the pair as "no one at all, from first to last". Either way the point is Job's: "No human knows what it is worth, and the land of the living does not have it" (Job 28:13). Wisdom, the law, is deeper than the sea (24:29), so no reader will ever finish studying it.

a: As for me
p: The "I" changes: now the teacher speaks of his own work as a small canal from Wisdom's great river.
b: In 24:3–22 "I" was Wisdom. From here to 24:34 the speaker is Ben Sira, as "for all who search for her" (24:34) shows: he is not Wisdom but her servant. His teaching is a ditch dug from her river to water a garden, his school. Then the ditch grows into a river and the river into a sea (24:31): his small work became more than he planned. The picture fits a teacher whose sayings were written down for students and, through his grandson's translation, carried far beyond Jerusalem.

a: an orchard
p: The Greek paradeisos means a park or orchard. It is the Greek Old Testament's word for the garden of Eden.
b: The Persian word for a walled park came into Greek as paradeisos. The Greek of Genesis uses it for the garden God planted in Eden (Genesis 2:8), and so it became the English "paradise". The Plain says "orchard" to keep the plain sense and to keep it apart from kēpos, "garden", in 24:31. But after the rivers of Eden in 24:25–27 a Greek reader would have heard the echo: the teacher's canal waters a new paradise.
r: Genesis 2:8–10; Ecclesiastes 2:5; Song of Songs 4:13; Luke 23:43; Revelation 2:7

a: my ditch became a river
p: The canal becomes a river and then a sea, like the stream from the temple in Ezekiel 47.
b: Ezekiel saw water flowing out from beneath the temple threshold, ankle deep, then knee deep, then a river no one could cross, and "life will come wherever the river goes" (Ezekiel 47:9). Ben Sira's image is smaller and personal: he meant to water his own garden, and the water outgrew him. Jewish and Christian readers have both used such images of teaching that keeps growing, and Jesus speaks of "rivers of living water" flowing from the one who believes (John 7:38).

a: as if it were prophecy
p: Ben Sira compares his teaching to prophecy. He does not claim to be a prophet, but he claims his words will last.
b: Agrees: wisdom teachers in Israel spoke with God-given insight (Proverbs 2:6), and Ben Sira's teaching rests on the law and the prophets. Goes beyond: he compares his own teaching to prophecy and expects it to last for every generation. A generation or two later, 1 Maccabees speaks of "the day a prophet was last seen among them" (1 Maccabees 9:27). Churches that read Sirach as Scripture take the line as fulfilled in the book's inspired authority. Anglicans read it, in Article VI's words, "for example of life and instruction of manners" but not "to establish any doctrine"; the Westminster Confession counts it among "other human writings".

a: I am made beautiful by three things
p: The Greek "beautiful" is feminine, as if Wisdom were still speaking. The Latin has "my spirit is pleased".
b: In anēstēn hōraia, "I stand beautiful", the adjective is feminine. Either Wisdom of chapter 24 goes on speaking, or the line once said something else and the Greek copy was confused. The Latin reads In tribus placitum est spiritui meo, "In three things my spirit is pleased", and the KJV has "In three things I was beautified". The Plain keeps the Greek. The saying is the first of several number sayings in these chapters (25:1–2, 7; 26:5, 28), a form Proverbs uses too.
orig: ἀνέστην ὡραία (anēstēn hōraia), 'I stood up beautiful' (feminine)

a: brothers who agree
p: Psalm 133 sings the same: how good it is when brothers live as one.
b: "Look how good it is, how lovely, when brothers live together, all as one!" (Psalm 133:1). Ben Sira's three lovely things all concern living together: brothers, neighbors, and husband and wife. The Greek homonoia, "being of one mind", was a common Greek word for harmony in a city; here it is the harmony of a family.

a: How lovely good judgment is in gray hair
p: Proverbs calls gray hair a crown. Ben Sira adds: only when wisdom comes with it.
b: "Gray hair is a crown of beauty, found by those who walk in righteousness" (Proverbs 16:31), and "old men's beauty is their gray hair" (Proverbs 20:29). Ben Sira makes the condition plain: what is lovely in the old is judgment, counsel and experience, and their "crown" is long experience, their boast the fear of the Lord (25:6). The verse before warns that this does not come by itself: what was not gathered in youth will not be found in old age (25:3).

a: who lives to see his enemies fall
p: Ben Sira counts it happy to see enemies fall. Proverbs warns against cheering, and Jesus says to love enemies.
b: Agrees: the Psalms often hope to see God's justice on the wicked (Psalm 54:7; Psalm 92:11). Tension: Proverbs warns, "When your enemy falls, do not be glad, and when he trips, keep your heart from cheering" (Proverbs 24:17), and Ben Sira himself says a trap will catch "those who are glad when godly people fall" (27:29). Jesus goes further: "keep loving your enemies" (Matthew 5:44). The Hebrew of this line (Manuscript C) reads "happy is the man who rejoices in his latter end, who lives and sees the breaking of his foes": the stress is on living long enough to see wrong set right.

a: who has not slipped with his tongue
p: A happy man has not slipped with his tongue, a theme Ben Sira returns to in 28:13–26. James says the same.
b: Ben Sira had already called happy the man who has not slipped with his mouth (14:1). James writes, "Whoever never trips in what he says is a complete man, able to bridle the whole body as well" (James 3:2). The long warning about the tongue in 28:13–26 spells out what such a slip can do.

a: The fear of the Lord
p: The book's great theme. The Greek has "Lord" where Proverbs' Hebrew has the name of God, so the Plain says "the Lord".
b: "The fear of the LORD is where knowledge begins" (Proverbs 1:7), and Ben Sira builds his book on that saying (1:11–20). Fear here is awe and reverence that leads to obedience, not terror. The Greek translation has Kyrios, "Lord", with no divine name, so the site writes "the Lord" in Sirach, not "the LORD". After the ten happy things, this is the summit: finding wisdom is great, but fearing the Lord is greater (25:10), because wisdom begins there.

a: Let it be any wound
p: The Greek leaves out the verb: "every wound, and not a wound of the heart". The Plain adds "Let it be".
b: Greek pasan plēgēn, kai mē plēgēn kardias is a short cry, as if the speaker says, "Bring me any wound, only not that one." The KJV supplied "Give me". The Hebrew of Manuscript C has a different sense, "Not every wound is like a wound of the heart; not every evil is like the evil of...", with the last word lost in a tear. Both forms make the heartache of a bad marriage the worst trouble a man can have, which is the theme of 25:13–26.
orig: πᾶσαν πληγήν, καὶ μὴ πληγὴν καρδίας (pasan plēgēn, kai mē plēgēn kardias)

a: Living with a lion and a dragon would suit me better
t: Better a lion than a quarrelsome wife
p: Proverbs says it is better to live on the roof or in the wilderness. Ben Sira sharpens it: better a lion and a dragon.
b: "Living in a corner up on the roof is better than a shared house with a woman who picks fights" (Proverbs 21:9; Proverbs 25:24), and "living out in the wilderness is better than living with a woman who quarrels and seethes" (Proverbs 21:19). These sayings, like Ben Sira's, are addressed to young men about choosing and living with a wife, and they are one side of a larger picture: the same teachers praise the good wife as God's gift (26:1–4; Proverbs 18:22; Proverbs 31:10–31).

a: If a wife pays her husband's way
t: When a wife supports her husband
p: Ben Sira calls it shame for a man to be supported by his wife. Proverbs 31 praises a wife who earns.
b: The Greek epichorēgē and the Hebrew mekhalkelet (Manuscript C) both mean to provide for, to keep. A wife with her own wealth who keeps her husband brings him, in Ben Sira's eyes, "anger, brazenness and deep shame": the shame is the man's loss of standing. Tension: Proverbs' woman of strength buys a field and "from the fruit of her palms she plants a vineyard" (Proverbs 31:16), and her husband is honored for it (Proverbs 31:23). Luke tells of women who supported Jesus and the Twelve from their own means (Luke 8:3). Ben Sira's line reflects the honor code of his class; the Bible does not make it a rule.

a: The beginning of sin came from a woman
t: The Greek and the Hebrew of 25:24
p: Both the Greek and the Hebrew say sin began from a woman and "we" die because of her.
b: The Greek reads apo gynaikos archē hamartias, kai di' autēn apothnēskomen pantes, "from a woman (or wife) is the beginning of sin, and through her we all die". The Hebrew of Manuscript C has the same thought: me'ishah techillat 'avon, uvighlalah gava'nu yachad, "from a woman is the beginning of guilt, and because of her we perish together". The Hebrew word for sin is 'avon, guilt or iniquity, and "we all" is "together". Greek gynē and Hebrew ishah both mean "woman" and "wife": the whole debate over this verse turns on that double meaning (see the next note).
orig: ἀπὸ γυναικὸς ἀρχὴ ἁμαρτίας (apo gynaikos archē hamartias); Hebrew מאשה תחלת עון ובגללה גוענו יחד

a: on account of her we all die
p: Most readers hear Eve and the fall. Others argue the verse is about the bad wife of 25:13–26.
b: Eve: the usual reading takes "a woman" as Eve, who took the fruit first (Genesis 3:6), and "we all die" as the death of every human (Genesis 3:19). Bullard and Hatton note that this is how the verse is usually read, beside 1 Timothy 2:13–14 and 2 Corinthians 11:3. The bad wife: Jack Levison argued that this is neither required nor correct. The verse sits in a poem about an evil wife (25:13–26), so "woman" means a wife and "we" means husbands: a bad wife leads her husband into sin and to an early grave, just as a good wife doubles his days (26:1). Bullard and Hatton find his case convincing. Teresa Ann Ellis returned to the question in 2011. The Plain keeps "a woman", which allows both readings, as the Greek does.

a: and on account of her we all die
p: Genesis blames both the man and the woman, and Paul says sin entered through one man. Read of Eve, this verse goes beyond both.
b: Genesis: the woman ate and "gave some to her husband too, who was there with her, and he ate" (Genesis 3:6); God holds both to account, and to Adam he says, "Since you obeyed your wife's voice", "the ground is cursed on your account" (Genesis 3:17). Paul: "sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin" (Romans 5:12): Adam, not Eve. 1 Timothy 2:14 says, "The woman was the one fooled through and through", but builds no teaching about death on it. Other Jewish answers: the Wisdom of Solomon says "death came into the world through the devil's envy" (Wisdom of Solomon 2:24). Verdict: if 25:24 speaks of Eve, it lays the beginning of sin on the woman alone, which goes beyond Genesis and conflicts with Paul's naming of Adam, whom Christian teaching on original sin follows. If it speaks of a bad wife (previous note), it is a harsh proverb about marriage, not about the fall.
r: Genesis 3:6; Genesis 3:17–19; Romans 5:12–19; 1 Corinthians 15:22; 1 Timothy 2:14; Wisdom of Solomon 2:24

a: we all die
t: Claude's observation: Ben Sira on where death comes from
p: Elsewhere Ben Sira treats death as the Creator's decree for all flesh, which fits the "bad wife" reading.
b: Claude's observation, not a published argument I have checked: twice Ben Sira speaks of death as part of how God made people, without mentioning a fall. In the Greek of 17:1 the Lord creates a human being out of earth and turns him back to it again, and in 41:4 death is the Lord's decree for all flesh. If he thought of death as the Creator's plan from the start, it is less likely that he meant 25:24 to explain death's origin by Eve's sin. That points toward Levison's contextual reading (previous notes), though Levison, as Bullard and Hatton report him, argues from the surrounding poem rather than from these verses. Against it: 40:1 calls the human race "sons of Adam", and Ben Sira could hold both thoughts at once.

a: Do not give water a way out
p: A leak in a cistern drains it dry. Proverbs uses the same picture for a quarrel.
b: In a dry land, water stored in a cistern was life; a crack let it all run out. "The start of a quarrel is like letting water loose, so before the fight breaks out, let it go" (Proverbs 17:14). Ben Sira applies the picture to a household: give an evil wife free power (the Greek of Vaticanus) or free speech (other Greek copies: see the variant), and the house drains away.

a: cut her away from your flesh
p: "Cut her away from your flesh" means divorce. The phrase undoes Genesis' "one flesh".
b: Husband and wife "become one flesh" (Genesis 2:24), so cutting a wife away from "your flesh" means ending the marriage. The Law allowed a man to divorce with a certificate (Deuteronomy 24:1), and the KJV's text adds "give her a bill of divorce" (see the variant). The Talmud quotes a related saying in Ben Sira's name: "A bad wife is leprosy for her husband. What is his remedy? He shall chase her from his house and will be healed from his leprosy" (Sanhedrin 100b, Davidson English). Compared with the Bible: Malachi says the LORD "hates sending away" (Malachi 2:16), and Jesus answers the divorce question with "What God has yoked together, then, no human being should separate" (Matthew 19:6), allowing divorce only for sexual sin (Matthew 19:9). Ben Sira's advice stands on the more permissive side of the debate Jesus addressed.

a: The man with a good wife is a happy man
p: The Talmud quotes this saying in Ben Sira's name, with "beautiful" for "good".
b: Although the rabbis did not count Ben Sira among the holy books, Rav Yosef says in the Babylonian Talmud that "we teach the superior matters that are in it", and the first examples are from this chapter: "A good wife is a good gift; she will be given into the bosom of a God-fearing man" (26:3) and "A beautiful wife, happy is her husband; the number of his days is doubled" (26:1), both in Sanhedrin 100b, with the same sayings in Yevamot 63b. The Hebrew of Manuscript C has "a good wife", like the Greek.

a: A wife of strength
p: The Greek "brave wife" stands for the Hebrew eshet chayil, Proverbs' "woman of strength".
b: The Greek gynē andreia means a brave or capable woman. Manuscript C has the Hebrew behind it, eshet chayil, the phrase of Proverbs 31:10, "A woman of strength, who can find one?", and of Proverbs 12:4, "A woman of strength is her husband's crown". The Plain uses the same English here and at 28:15, where the same Greek words return. In the Hebrew the second line also differs: she "makes her husband prosper" (literally "makes him fat").
orig: γυνὴ ἀνδρεία (gynē andreia); Hebrew אשת חיל (eshet chayil)

a: those who fear the Lord
p: Here the Hebrew writes the divine name in short, three letters yod, where the Greek has "Lord".
b: Manuscript C reads uvchelek yere' YYY tinnaten, "and in the portion of one who fears the LORD she will be given". The three yods were a Jewish scribe's way of writing the name YHWH without spelling it out. Where this copy has the name, the grandson's Greek, like the whole Greek Bible, puts Kyrios, "Lord". Since the Plain translates the Greek, it keeps "the Lord" here. The Talmud quotes the line as "she will be given into the bosom of a God-fearing man" (Sanhedrin 100b).
orig: ירא ייי (yere' YYY), 'one who fears the LORD'

a: My heart shrinks back from three things
p: Three public dangers and a fourth at home: the worst of them is a jealous wife (26:6).
b: Ben Sira uses the "three, and a fourth" pattern of Proverbs 30. The three are dangers of public life in a city: slander that spreads through the town, a mob, and false accusation, "all worse than death". The fourth, in 26:6, is a jealous wife. In Vaticanus Ben Sira says that before the fourth he "pleaded"; other copies say "I was afraid" (see the variant).

a: a wife who is jealous of a rival wife
p: In a household with two wives, rivalry was a known misery, as Hannah and Peninnah show.
b: The Greek antizēlos is a rival, and here it means a second wife in the same house. Ben Sira's world still allowed a man more than one wife, though most men had one. The Bible tells the cost: Hannah's "rival taunted her cruelly" (1 Samuel 1:6), Sarah and Hagar quarreled (Genesis 16:4–6), and Rachel and Leah competed for Jacob (Genesis 30:1–24). The Law forbade marrying a woman's sister "as a rival" while she lived (Leviticus 18:18).

a: an ox yoke that shakes loose
p: A yoke that slips and chafes makes the team pull badly. Paul uses the yoke for marriage too.
b: A yoke joined two oxen to pull together; if it shakes loose, it rubs them raw and the plowing goes wrong. Ben Sira makes an evil wife such a yoke, and holding her a scorpion in the hand. The Hebrew of 25:8 (Manuscript C) already warned against plowing "with an ox and a donkey together", the rule of Deuteronomy 22:10, as a picture of a bad match. Paul uses the same picture: "Do not hitch yourselves to unbelievers in a yoke that does not match" (2 Corinthians 6:14).

a: sexual sin
p: The Greek porneia is the broad word for sexual wrongdoing.
b: Porneia covers every kind of sexual sin, and the site renders it "sexual sin" across the Bible. Ben Sira says it shows in a woman's roving, upward glances and in her eyelids, as Proverbs warns of the adulteress who will "catch you with her eyelids" (Proverbs 6:25).

a: a daughter
p: In Ben Sira's world a daughter's sexual reputation was her family's honor. He returns to this worry in 42:9–14.
b: A father arranged his daughter's marriage, and her virginity at marriage was a matter of the family's honor and of law (Deuteronomy 22:13–21). Ben Sira writes as a father to fathers, and in 42:9 he says that a daughter keeps her father awake with worry; the Talmud quotes that passage in Ben Sira's name (Sanhedrin 100b). The Plain gives his words as they stand. Readers will notice that the guard is set on the daughter, not on the men around her.

a: opens her quiver for any arrow
p: The thirsty traveler, the tent peg and the quiver are pictures of sexual behavior, as readers of the time knew.
b: The verse uses images rather than plain words: drinking from any water nearby (compare Proverbs 5:15, "Drink the water your own cistern holds"), sitting before every tent peg, and opening the quiver to any arrow are all ways of speaking of a woman who gives herself to any man. The Plain keeps the images, since the Greek does, and does not make them cruder or softer. The subject is the shameless daughter or woman of 26:10–11.
orig: ἔναντι βέλους ἀνοίξει φαρέτραν (enanti belous anoixei pharetran), 'before an arrow she will open a quiver'

a: A quiet wife is the Lord's gift
p: Ben Sira praises a quiet, well-taught wife, as 1 Peter praises "a gentle and calm spirit".
b: Proverbs says "a wife with good sense comes from the LORD" (Proverbs 19:14), and 1 Peter urges wives to be adorned with "a gentle and calm spirit. That is worth a great deal to God" (1 Peter 3:4). Ben Sira's sigēra means "silent" or "quiet"; the second line praises a "well-taught soul". He prizes a wife's education as well as her quiet: the Greek pepaideumenē is "trained, educated".

a: a self-controlled soul
p: The Hebrew of Manuscript C praises a wife who keeps her mouth shut; the Greek says "self-controlled soul".
b: Manuscript C reads ve'ein mishqal litsrorat peh, "there is no weight (price) for one who keeps her mouth tied up", that is, a woman who can keep a secret or hold her tongue. The Greek turns this into enkratēs psychē, "a self-controlled soul", a phrase Greek moral writers would have known. The Latin and the KJV ("her continent mind") follow the Greek.
orig: ἐγκρατοῦς ψυχῆς (enkratous psychēs); Hebrew צרורת פה (tserorat peh), 'one tied up at the mouth'

a: The sun as it climbs in the Lord's high places
p: The Greek sets each picture beside a good wife without "like" or "so", the way Hebrew proverbs often do.
b: Verses 16–18 put two things side by side and let the reader see the likeness: the rising sun and a good wife's beauty, the temple lamp and a lovely face, the golden pillars and shapely feet. The Plain keeps that form. Many translations add "like... so". All three pictures come from the sanctuary and the sky: the sun "in the Lord's high places", the holy lampstand (26:17), and gold set on silver bases as in the tabernacle (Exodus 26:19). The Hebrew of Manuscript C even places the good wife bidvir, "in the inner room", using devir, the word for the temple's inner sanctuary.
orig: ἥλιος ἀνατέλλων... καὶ κάλλος (hēlios anatellōn... kai kallos), 'the sun rising... and beauty'
r: Exodus 25:31; Exodus 26:19; Song of Songs 5:15; Proverbs 31:10–31

a: My child
p: The Greek teknon is "child". The KJV has "My son". This passage is only in the longer Greek.
b: Ben Sira addresses his student as teknon, "child", throughout the book, and the site renders it "my child". Proverbs' Hebrew has beni, "my son" (Proverbs 1:8), and the KJV has "My son" here. There is no Hebrew for 26:19–27: the whole passage belongs to the longer form of the Greek and is not in Vaticanus or the Latin (see the variants).

a: sow your own seed there
p: The field is the wife, the seed is children: marry well, stay faithful, and your line will last.
b: The point is the one of Proverbs 5: "Drink the water your own cistern holds" and "take your joy from the woman you married when you were young" (Proverbs 5:15, 18). Do not waste your strength on strangers (26:19); choose a good wife, be faithful to her, and your children will carry on a good name (26:21).

a: The man with a good wife is a happy man
p: The longer Greek repeats the saying of 26:1 here, with "years" for "days". The Plain repeats the English too.
b: The extra lines in this verse echo 26:1 almost word for word. A scribe who added the passage of 26:19–27 seems to have rounded it off with the saying that begins the chapter. The Plain gives both lines in the same English so the repetition can be seen.
orig: γυναικὸς ἀγαθῆς μακάριος ὁ ἀνήρ (gynaikos agathēs makarios ho anēr)

a: The Lord will make him ready for the sword
p: The worst of the three: the righteous who turns to sin. Ezekiel says the same.
b: Of three things that anger Ben Sira, two are wrongs done to good men (a soldier left poor, sensible men despised), but the third is a man's own choice: "one who leaves what is right and goes back to sin". Agrees: Ezekiel says, "when a righteous person turns away from his righteousness and does injustice... None of the righteous deeds he did will be remembered" (Ezekiel 18:24). Christians differ on whether one who truly believes can fall away for good; that question is set out on the topic page.

a: a shopkeeper
p: The kapēlos was a small trader or innkeeper. Vaticanus' first scribe wrote "camel".
b: Ben Sira does not condemn trade, but he thinks it hard to buy and sell without cheating (27:2). The kapēlos was a retailer, a seller of small goods or wine. Swete's notes show that the first hand of Codex Vaticanus wrote kamēlos, "camel", a slip of one letter that a corrector fixed. The prophets had already accused the merchants of Israel: "We will make the ephah small and the shekel large" (Amos 8:5).

a: sin will be ground in between selling and buying
p: As a peg is jammed between stones, sin is jammed into every deal. The prophets said the same of Israel's markets.
b: Ben Sira's picture is of a wooden peg driven into the crack between building stones: once in, it does not come out. So sin gets ground into buying and selling. The Law demanded honest weights (Deuteronomy 25:13–15), Proverbs says "Scales that cheat are abhorrent to the LORD" (Proverbs 11:1), and Amos heard merchants say, "We will make the ephah small and the shekel large, and cheat with scales that lie" (Amos 8:5). Ben Sira does not forbid trade; he warns that only the fear of the Lord keeps a merchant's house standing (27:3).

a: Shake a sieve and the rubbish stays in it
p: Three tests in a row: the sieve, the potter's furnace, the fruit. Each shows what a person is by how he talks.
b: When grain is shaken in a sieve, the good grain falls through and the rubbish stays on top for all to see. A potter's jars go into the furnace, and the firing shows which will crack. A tree's fruit shows how it was tended. In each case the test is speech: a person's reasoning and talk show what is in him. The furnace picture is also in Proverbs: "Silver goes in the melting pot and gold in the furnace, but it is the LORD who puts hearts to the test" (Proverbs 17:3).

a: The fruit shows how a tree was tended
p: Jesus uses the same picture: a tree is known by its fruit, and the mouth speaks what fills the heart.
b: "You will know who they are from their fruit" (Matthew 7:16); "You can tell a tree by its fruit" (Matthew 12:33), and in the same passage, "What overflows from the heart is what the mouth speaks" (Matthew 12:34). Ben Sira joins the same two thoughts: the fruit shows the tree's care, and a man's words show the thoughts of his heart. Jesus applies the saying to prophets and teachers; Ben Sira, to anyone whose character is being judged. The likeness shows a shared Jewish proverb; it does not prove that one borrowed from the other.

a: an ankle-length robe of glory
p: The Greek podērēs, "reaching to the feet", is the high priest's robe in the Greek Exodus.
b: Righteousness is pictured as a robe that reaches to the ankles. The same Greek word is used in the Greek of Exodus for Aaron's robe (Exodus 28:4), in the Wisdom of Solomon of the high priest Aaron's "ankle-length robe" (Wisdom of Solomon 18:24), and in Revelation of the risen Christ, who "wore a robe that came down to his feet" (Revelation 1:13). Isaiah and Job also speak of putting on righteousness like a garment (Isaiah 61:10; Job 29:14).
orig: ποδήρη δόξης (podērē doxēs), 'a foot-length robe of glory'
r: Exodus 28:4; Wisdom of Solomon 18:24; Revelation 1:13; Isaiah 61:10; Job 29:14; 45:8

a: A lion sets an ambush for its prey
p: Sin waits like a lion for wrongdoers, as God told Cain that sin was crouching at his door.
b: God warned Cain, "sin is crouching at the door. Its desire is for you, but you must rule over it" (Genesis 4:7). Ben Sira's lion is the same idea: sin is not only something a person does but a hunter that catches those who keep doing wrong. 1 Peter uses the lion for the devil, "walking about like a lion that roars, looking for someone to gulp down" (1 Peter 5:8).

a: a fool keeps changing, like the moon
p: The moon is never the same two nights running. James pictures the double-minded as a wave.
b: The moon waxes and wanes; the fool's talk and mind are just as unsteady. James has a similar warning: "a person who wavers is like an ocean wave that the wind whips up and throws about", "a double-minded man, never steady on any road he takes" (James 1:6, 8). The Latin adds a contrast: "A holy man continueth in wisdom as the sun" (Vulgate 27:12, Douay).

a: keep an eye on the time
p: Literally "keep the time": in foolish company, watch for the moment to leave.
b: The Greek syntērēson kairon, "keep (watch for) the right time", is the opposite of the second line's endelechize, "keep on, stay". With people who have no sense, look for the moment to leave; with thoughtful people, stay as long as you can. The Latin reads it differently, "keep in the word till its time" (Vulgate 27:13, Douay), that is, keep quiet until the right moment.

a: someone who swears oaths all the time
p: Constant swearing by God's name is a theme in Ben Sira (23:9–11). Jesus says not to swear at all.
b: The Greek polyorkos is a man who swears many oaths, calling on God's name to back up every word. Ben Sira had warned his student not to get his mouth used to oaths (23:9). Jesus says, "do not take oaths at all" (Matthew 5:34), and James, "do not take oaths, whether by heaven or by earth or with any other oath" (James 5:12). The third commandment stands behind them all (Exodus 20:7).

a: Whoever tells secrets has ruined trust
p: Proverbs makes the same point twice: the gossip lays bare what was said in confidence.
b: "One who goes around telling tales lays bare what was said in confidence, but one with a faithful spirit keeps the matter under cover" (Proverbs 11:13; compare Proverbs 20:19). Ben Sira gives the cost: a friendship lost like a bird let out of the hand or a gazelle out of a trap (27:19–20). In 22:22 he had said that a friend can be won back after many things, but not after a secret given away; here he says that such a man "has lost all hope" (27:21).

a: A man who winks
p: Winking was the sign of a man with a hidden plan, as Proverbs says.
b: Proverbs describes the troublemaker: "He winks with his eyes, shuffles his feet, and points his fingers" (Proverbs 6:13), and "One who winks an eye causes pain" (Proverbs 10:10). The wink is a secret signal to an ally while the victim is smiled at. Ben Sira describes the same man: sweet to your face, twisted behind your back (27:23). The KJV's text has a different second line: "he that knoweth him will depart from him".

a: The one who digs a pit falls into it
p: Ben Sira repeats Proverbs 26:27, and the Plain repeats Proverbs' wording.
b: "The one who digs a pit falls into it, and the stone comes back on the one who rolls it" (Proverbs 26:27); Ecclesiastes has "The one who digs a pit falls into it" too (Ecclesiastes 10:8), and the psalm says of the wicked, "He dug a pit and hollowed it out, and into the ditch he made he has fallen" (Psalm 7:15). Ben Sira gathers the whole set: the stone thrown up that lands on the thrower (27:25), the pit, the trap, and evil that rolls back (27:27). Esther tells a whole story of it: Haman hangs on the pole he set up for Mordecai (Esther 7:10).

a: those who are glad when godly people fall
p: Those who gloat over the fall of the godly fall into a trap themselves.
b: Proverbs warns, "When your enemy falls, do not be glad" (Proverbs 24:17), and Obadiah says to Edom, "Do not look on with delight at your brother's day, the day of his misfortune" (Obadiah 12). Here the gloating is at the fall of the godly, which makes it worse. Compare Ben Sira's own happy man who "lives to see his enemies fall" (25:7): there it is God's justice on enemies, here it is joy at the suffering of the good.

a: Fury and anger are abhorrent things too
p: Ben Sira uses the strong word the Bible uses for what God detests.
b: The Greek bdelygmata renders the Hebrew to'evah, which the site translates "abhorrent": the word used of idols and of practices God detests (Proverbs 11:1; Deuteronomy 7:25). To call anger abhorrent is to put it beside such things. The verse begins the passage on anger and forgiveness that runs to 28:7. Jesus also treats anger as a sin that brings judgment (Matthew 5:22).

a: The one who takes revenge will find revenge from the Lord
p: Revenge belongs to God. Those who take it for themselves will meet his.
b: The Law says, "Do not take vengeance, and do not keep a grudge against the children of your people. You are to love your neighbor as yourself" (Leviticus 19:18), and the Song of Moses, "Vengeance belongs to me, and payback" (Deuteronomy 32:35). Paul quotes it: "never take revenge yourselves, but make room for the anger" (Romans 12:19). Ben Sira adds a warning: the one who takes revenge will have his own sins held "firmly fixed" by God, kept on record rather than forgiven.

a: Forgive the wrong your neighbor did to you
p: The closest saying before Jesus to "forgive us... as we have forgiven" in the Lord's Prayer.
b: Agrees: Jesus taught, "forgive us the debts we owe, just as we ourselves have forgiven the people who owe us" (Matthew 6:12), and "If you forgive people their wrongs, you too will be forgiven by your heavenly Father" (Matthew 6:14). Mark: "whenever you are standing in prayer and you have a complaint against anyone, forgive him" (Mark 11:25). Ben Sira ties forgiveness to prayer in the same way, and argues for it (28:3–5): how can one who keeps anger ask God for healing? Goes further in Jesus: the parable of the unforgiving slave (Matthew 18:23–35) makes God's forgiveness come first, so that forgiving others is the response to mercy received. Christians of every tradition hear the Lord's Prayer in this verse.
r: Matthew 6:12–15; Mark 11:25; Matthew 18:21–35; Luke 6:37; Colossians 3:13; Ephesians 4:32

a: your own sins will be released
p: The Greek verb means to untie or set loose: forgiveness as being freed from a bond.
b: Ben Sira's grandson uses lythēsontai, "they will be loosed", not the usual word for forgiving. Sin is pictured as a cord or debt that holds a person; God unties it. The same picture appears in Isaiah, "to unlock the fetters of wickedness, to loosen the ropes of the yoke" (Isaiah 58:6), and in Revelation 1:5, where the critical Greek text has lysanti, "set free" (the site's Plain: "who set us free from our sins with his blood"), while the Byzantine text and the KJV have "washed".

a: does he look to the Lord for healing
p: Sin is pictured as sickness, and forgiveness as being healed, as in the psalms.
b: "LORD, be kind to me; heal my very self, because I have sinned against you" (Psalm 41:4). Hosea promises, "I will heal their turning away" (Hosea 14:4), and Isaiah says of the servant, "by his welts healing came to us" (Isaiah 53:5). Ben Sira asks how a person who nurses anger can expect such healing from God, and in 28:5 how such a one can expect anyone to make atonement for him. He speaks as one who believed atonement was real: at the temple (50:5–21) and through mercy shown to the poor (3:30).

a: Remember the last things
p: In Ben Sira "the last things" are your own end: decay and death. Christian readers heard the four last things.
b: The Greek ta eschata means "the last things" or "your end", and the second line spells it out: "decay and death". Ben Sira says the same in 7:36, "in all your words remember your end". Agrees: "Teach us, then, to count our days, so that we may bring in a wise heart" (Psalm 90:12); death is a reason to let go of hatred. Goes beyond in Christian reading: the Latin reads Memento novissimorum, "Remember thy last things" (Douay), and Christian readers could hear in it the "four last things" of Catholic teaching: death, judgment, heaven and hell. Ben Sira himself says little here about a judgment after death; his warning is that life is short.

a: let mistakes go
p: The Greek says "overlook ignorance": wrongs done without knowing, the unintentional sins of the Law.
b: The Greek paride agnoian means "overlook what was done in ignorance". The Law separated sins done by mistake from sins done defiantly (Leviticus 4:2; Numbers 15:27–31). Ben Sira asks his student to treat a neighbor's faults as mistakes, the way the Most High's covenant does. From the cross Jesus kept saying, "Father, forgive them, because they do not know what they are doing" (Luke 23:34).

a: Blow on a spark and it bursts into flame
p: The same mouth can fan a quarrel or put it out. James uses the same contrast.
b: Blowing on a spark and spitting on it both come from your mouth: you choose whether a quarrel grows or dies. James writes, "From one and the same mouth pour blessing and curse. It is not right, my brothers, for things to go this way" (James 3:10), and "See how little a flame it takes to set a huge forest alight!" (James 3:5). Proverbs adds, "When the wood runs out, the fire dies, and when there is no gossip, the fighting calms down" (Proverbs 26:20).

a: The tongue of a third party
p: The Greek "third tongue" renders a Hebrew idiom for slander: talk about someone who is not there.
b: The Greek glōssa tritē, "a third tongue", makes no sense in Greek, and a later hand's note in the margin of Vaticanus tried trētē, "pierced". It is a Hebrew phrase. The Talmud quotes a saying from the land of Israel: "Third speech, i.e., malicious speech about a third party, kills three people": the one who speaks it, the one who accepts it, and the one about whom it is said (Arakhin 15b). The Plain says "the tongue of a third party" to keep the idiom. The Latin keeps it word for word, lingua tertia.

a: wives of strength
p: The same Greek as 26:2: good, strong wives sent away because of lies told about them.
b: "Wives of strength" is the same Greek, gynaikas andreias, as "a wife of strength" in 26:2. Slander has driven such women out, that is, made their husbands divorce them, and taken from them the fruit of their work. The Law already guarded a wife against a husband's false charge (Deuteronomy 22:13–19).

a: a tongue's lash breaks bones
p: Proverbs says a soft tongue breaks bone. Ben Sira turns it around: a cruel tongue breaks bones too.
b: "A ruler is won over by slowness to anger, and a soft tongue breaks bone" (Proverbs 25:15) praises gentle speech that breaks down resistance. Ben Sira uses the bone image for the harm of words: a whip leaves welts on the skin, but a lashing tongue goes deeper, to the bones.

a: The sword's mouth
p: "The mouth of the sword" is the Hebrew way of saying its edge. The pun with the tongue is the point.
b: The Greek en stomati machairas, "by the mouth of the sword", copies the Hebrew pi cherev, the usual phrase for a sword's edge. Here it plays against the tongue, which also lives in a mouth: the sword's mouth has killed many, but the tongue in a person's mouth has killed more. Revelation pictures the risen Christ with a sharp sword coming out of his mouth (Revelation 1:16), the word that judges.
orig: ἐν στόματι μαχαίρας (en stomati machairas), 'by the mouth of a sword'

a: its yoke is an iron yoke
p: The tongue's power is pictured as the iron yoke of a conqueror, as in Jeremiah.
b: Jeremiah warned the nations: "I have put a yoke of iron on the neck of all these nations, to serve Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon" (Jeremiah 28:14), and Deuteronomy threatened an iron yoke for the disobedient (Deuteronomy 28:48). Slander is a tyrant: those who fall under it are bound as captives. The opposite is Wisdom's yoke, which Ben Sira will urge his students to take on (51:26).

a: Hades would be more welcome than that
p: Hades is the Greek name for Sheol, the world of the dead. Death there is better than life under slander.
b: The Greek Old Testament uses Hades for the Hebrew Sheol, the shadowy place where all the dead go. Ben Sira does not speak of hell as punishment here: he means that plain death and the grave would be better than the slow "evil death" that slander brings. On his view of the dead, compare 41:4, where there is no arguing about life's length in Hades.

a: it will blaze inside them and never go out
t: A fire that is not put out
p: The words recall Isaiah 66:24 and Jesus' warnings about Gehenna, but here the fire is the tongue's.
b: Isaiah ends with the bodies of rebels whose "fire will not be put out" (Isaiah 66:24), and Jesus uses the same words of Gehenna, "where their worm never dies and the fire is never put out" (Mark 9:48). James says the tongue "sets fire to the wheel of existence, and Gehenna sets it on fire" (James 3:6). Compared with the Bible: Ben Sira's fire is the destruction slander brings on those who abandon the Lord, in this life. He does not speak of punishment after death here; the New Testament passages do.

a: a door and a bar
p: Guard your words as carefully as your money: weigh them, and put a door and a bar on your mouth.
b: As you would fence in a field and tie up silver and gold (28:24), weigh your words on a scale and lock your mouth. The psalm prays, "LORD, post a guard for my mouth; stand watch over the door of my lips" (Psalm 141:3), and Proverbs says, "Watch your mouth and your tongue, and you keep your life out of troubles" (Proverbs 21:23).

a: Be careful not to slip up with it
p: "It" is the tongue, feminine in Greek like the tongue of 28:13–23.
b: The Greek en autē, "in it" or "by it", is feminine and refers back to the tongue (glōssa) that the whole passage has been about. The warning closes the section: guard your words or you will fall in front of an enemy who is waiting for your slip. The KJV's "by it" keeps the same unclear pronoun.

a: Whoever shows mercy will lend to his neighbor
p: In the Law, lending to a neighbor in need is a duty and an act of mercy. Jesus goes further.
b: Agrees: the Law commands, "open your hand wide to him, and lend him enough for whatever he lacks" (Deuteronomy 15:8), and forbids interest from a poor brother (Exodus 22:25; Leviticus 25:36). The righteous man "is generous and lends" (Psalm 37:26). Ben Sira calls lending "keeping the commandments", and he expects the borrower to repay (29:2). Goes beyond in Jesus: "keep loving your enemies, doing good, and lending without hoping for anything back" (Luke 6:35).
r: Deuteronomy 15:7–11; Exodus 22:25; Leviticus 25:35–37; Psalm 37:26; Psalm 112:5; Luke 6:34–35

a: pays back in tired excuses
p: The borrower "pays back" not money but words. The Greek word for them is akēdia, weariness.
b: The Greek says he "will pay back words of akēdia": careless, bored, couldn't-care-less words. Later Christian monks used akēdia ("acedia") for the listless sloth that keeps a person from prayer. The picture of the borrower is sharp and comic: humble and hand-kissing until he has the money, then full of delays and blaming "the times".

a: waiting for alms
p: Elēemosynē, a gift of mercy to the poor. The site uses "alms" for it, as in Tobit and Acts.
b: The Greek elēemosynē comes from eleos, "mercy", and means a gift given out of mercy to someone in need; English "alms" comes from it. In Ben Sira, giving alms is one of the great duties of a righteous person (3:30; 7:10; 29:8–13). The site renders the word "alms" in every book, as in Tobit and Acts.

a: Because the commandment says so
p: The commandment is Deuteronomy 15: open your hand to the poor brother.
b: "Open your hand wide to your brother, to the poor and the needy among you in your land" (Deuteronomy 15:11). Ben Sira gives no reason but this: the Law commands it. Proverbs adds a promise: "Showing kindness to a poor man is a loan made to the LORD, and he will pay him back for what he did" (Proverbs 19:17).

a: rust away under a rock
p: Better to lose money helping a brother than to bury it until it rusts. James and Jesus use the same picture.
b: People hid money and valuables under stones or in the ground, as the slave in Jesus' parable "hid your talent in the ground" (Matthew 25:25). Ben Sira says such money is lost anyway; spent on a brother or friend, it is not. James warns the rich, "Your gold and silver are eaten through with rust, and that rust will be a witness against you" (James 5:3), and Jesus: "Here moths and rust eat them away" (Matthew 6:19).

a: Store up your treasure as the Most High commands
p: Giving to the poor is a treasure stored with God, as Tobit and Jesus also teach.
b: Tobit tells his son that giving alms is "a good deposit for yourself, ready for the day of hard need" (Tobit 4:9). Jesus says, "pile up treasures for yourselves in heaven" (Matthew 6:20), and tells the rich man that if he gives to the poor he will have treasure in heaven (Matthew 19:21). Whether such giving earns merit before God, or is the fruit of faith in God's grace, is a question on which Christians differ; the "Where Christians differ" card at Tobit 4 sets out the views, and it is not repeated here.

a: alms will rescue you from every harm
p: Ben Sira promises that alms will protect the giver. Tobit says the same, and Daniel told a king to break with sin by mercy.
b: Agrees: Daniel advised Nebuchadnezzar, "Break with your sins by doing what is right, and with your wrongs by showing mercy to the poor" (Daniel 4:27), and Proverbs promises that God repays kindness to the poor (Proverbs 19:17). Goes beyond: "alms rescue from death" (Tobit 4:10) and "they cleanse away every sin" (Tobit 12:9) go further than the 66 books say, and Ben Sira's own 3:30 says alms atone for sins. The Latin of this verse is different: "Shut up alms in the heart of the poor, and it shall obtain help for thee against all evil" (Vulgate 29:15, Douay). The question of merit is on the Tobit 4 card.

a: A good man will stand good for his neighbor
p: Proverbs warns against guaranteeing others' debts. Ben Sira says a good man does it, and then warns of the risk.
b: To "stand good for" someone is to guarantee his loan, to promise to pay if he does not. Proverbs warns again and again: "Stand good for an outsider's loan, and you will be badly hurt" (Proverbs 11:15; Proverbs 6:1–5; Proverbs 17:18; Proverbs 22:26). Goes beyond: Ben Sira calls it what a good man does for a neighbor (29:14–15), and Judah offered himself so for Benjamin: "I will be his guarantor" (Genesis 43:9). Agrees: he then lists how it ruins people (29:18–19) and ends with the balance, "Help your neighbor as far as you are able" (29:20).

a: Never forget what your guarantor did for you
p: Hebrews calls Jesus the guarantor of a better covenant, with the same Greek word.
b: The Greek engyos, "guarantor", is the word Hebrews uses of Christ: "Jesus has become the one who guarantees a better covenant" (Hebrews 7:22). Paul offers himself as guarantor for the slave Onesimus: "if he is in your debt, put it on my account. ... I myself will repay" (Philemon 18–19). Ben Sira's "he put his life up for you" (literally "he gave his soul for you") describes a guarantor who risks all he has; Christian readers have heard more in it, though Ben Sira speaks of loans.

a: What life needs first is water, bread and clothing
p: Water, bread, clothing and a roof: what a person needs, as 1 Timothy says.
b: "If we have food and covering, we will count that enough" (1 Timothy 6:8). Jesus tells his followers to stop worrying about "what you will eat or what you will drink, or about your body, what you will put on" (Matthew 6:25). Ben Sira's point leads somewhere specific: better a poor home of your own than living off others (29:22–28).

a: Better to live poor under a shelter of beams
p: A Proverbs-style "better than" saying: a poor roof of your own over rich food at another's table.
b: "A plate of vegetables with love at the table is better than a stall-fed ox served with hatred" (Proverbs 15:17), and "A dry bit of bread with quiet is better than a house stuffed with sacrificial feasts and fighting" (Proverbs 17:1). Ben Sira's version is about independence: the man who lives off another's table pays for it in insults (29:24–28).

a: wherever a man lodges as a stranger
p: The Greek word is for a resident alien, someone living in a place without a home of his own.
b: Paroikeō and paroikos, "to live as an alien" and "resident alien", are the Greek Bible's words for people like Abraham, "a foreigner living among you as a settler" (Genesis 23:4), and 1 Peter calls Christians "resident aliens and temporary residents" (1 Peter 2:11). Here the word means a man who has no house of his own and must lodge with others, and so must keep quiet. The Plain says "lodger" in 29:26–27 for the same word.
orig: παροικήσει (paroikēsei), 'he will live as an alien'

a: an honored guest is here
t: Pushed out by a better guest
p: The host throws the lodger out to make room for his brother. Jesus warns against taking the best seat.
b: Ben Sira paints the life of a dependent guest: made to serve and pour the wine (29:25), ordered to set the table, then sent out when someone more important arrives. Jesus' advice at a banquet runs the other way: "go and recline in the last place, so that when the man who invited you comes, he will tell you, 'Friend, come up higher'" (Luke 14:10). The New Testament urges hosts, "Do not forget to welcome strangers" (Hebrews 13:2).

a: being insulted by a lender
p: The chapter ends where it began: the misery of debt, now from the borrower's side.
b: The Greek danistēs is a lender or creditor. The chapter opened with the duty to lend (29:1–2) and the borrower who will not repay (29:4–7); it ends with the shame of the man who depends on others for food and room and must take their insults. Ben Sira's advice through the whole chapter is to be generous, careful and, as far as possible, independent.
